chapter: N'goma drums and the scrapbook clippings
title: Kline reads the 1938 article on the N'goma drums: African inspiration
summary: Next morning Kline reads a Sunday Mirror clipping describing the N'goma drums, inspired by a survey of African music for NBC and adapted to jazz.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Early drum kits and the gear drummers used

blocks.x: It's the morning, the next morning, February 13th. Chauncey and Virginia are asleep. I have his book of letters, clippings, photographs, they very kindly let me look through. I thought before they wake up, I might read some of these clippings that perhaps the Institute would be interested in. There is an article here from the Sunday

Mirror, June 5, 1938. It discusses Chauncey's N'goma drums. We discussed these briefly last night off tape. He didn't remember where he got the name N'goma. That's capital N as in nothing, apostrophe, and then small g-o-m-a. They were the focus of his own band that he had in the thirties. I'll read this article very quickly.

The headline is "African Rhythm in Drum Device." It is a far cry from the primitive blatant beating of African tom toms to the raucous swinging tempos of our present day jazz tribes in cafes and ballrooms. Yet by an ingenius device invented by Chauncey Morehouse, orchestra leader, authentic African rhythms, the basic foundation of all swing music has been injected into American jazz. Morehouse has contributed the newest innovation in the music world, the N'goma drums. It is an instrument of his own design which consists of routine snare drums of varying sizes which are tuned chromatically, making it possible for the first time in musical history to play melody as well as rhythm on a percussion instrument. "The three year labor put into the construction of this instrument," explains Morehouse, "was inspired by the necessity to relieve swing music of the monotonous four-four tempo. By adding a melodic tone to its rhythm, the tempo can become musical. Many thought the instrument would be impractical but I think our recent phonograph recording proved it to be an advantageous feature to swing music." Morehouse first conceived the idea while making a survey of African music for the NBC Music

Library. In the Belgian Congo, he learned that a tribe known for its elaborate drum music, the natives used no melody instruments but contrived their music from intricate drum sets. In a New York public library, he also discovered music manuscripts of original African chants and adapted this native music to modern jazz interpretation. "Swing music for the main part," said Morehouse, "is improvised notes because the Africans had no way of writing their music, it was handed down from father to son and each generation sang and played its own interpretation of the melodies. In our music, this is known as ad libbing and is the most important phase of jazz occurring in every orchestra performance. The flexibility of the African songs made them suitable to jazz compositions such as 'Mazi-Pani*' and 'Ku-li-a' which we recently recorded." These two compositions were created by Morehouse. Mazi-Pani is a working song, comparable to early American railroad ditties and translated freely means, I do not like a man who is lying down. Ku-li-a is a hunting song sung in celebration of a big kill and means here is food to eat. When questioned further about the construction of N'goma, of his N'goma drums, Morehouse explained that his big problem in designing them was obtaining skins or drum heads the thickness of which would be in proportion to the size of the particular drum.
